A 3D diagram showing the concept of GIS layers. At the bottom, a flat, real-world satellite image of a landscape. Above it, several transparent square layers hover, stacked one on top of the other, pulled apart vertically so each is visible. The bottom layer shows blue polygons representing lakes and rivers (Water). The next layer up shows green polygons for forests (Vegetation). The next shows red and grey blocks for houses and buildings (Structures). The top layer shows grey lines for roads (Transportation). A vertical dashed line passes through all layers to show how they align perfectly over the same geographic location.

A split diagram comparing raster and vector data models. On the left (Raster), a house, a river, and a tree are represented by a grid of small coloured squares (pixels). The curves are jagged because they are made of blocks. On the right (Vector), the same house is drawn with sharp geometric lines and points (polygons), the river is a smooth curving line, and the tree is a precise point.

Two-panel illustration of GIS data capture. Left panel (Map Scanning): a physical paper map of a coastline is sliding through a wide, flat electronic scanner, coming out on a computer screen as a single flat image file. Right panel (Map Digitizing): a person's hand holds a mouse-like device with a crosshair (a puck) and traces the outline of a river on a paper map attached to a large flat electronic board (digitizing tablet). On the connected computer screen, a sharp red vector line appears exactly matching the traced river.
